turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi, thanks for coming in today. What's been going on for you lately?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's just, you know, same old stuff. I'm trying to get some projects done, but I end up getting sidetracked by, uh, this really cool YouTube video I saw last night. And then I'm like, "Oh, I should really watch that whole thing," and next thing I know, hours have passed. I'm just bad at adulting, you know?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you're struggling with procrastination and maybe some difficulty with self-regulation. It's like you're getting caught up in the instant gratification of watching that video, and it's hard to tear yourself away from it.

First of all, let me just say that you're not alone in this. Many people struggle with procrastination, and it's not necessarily about being "bad" at adulting. It's more about understanding what's driving your behavior and finding ways to work with it.

Can you tell me more about what's going on when you get sidetracked? Is it just the YouTube video, or are there other things that distract you too? And what are some of the projects you're trying to get done, but having trouble with? 

Also, have you noticed any patterns or triggers that might contribute to your procrastination? For example, do you tend to get sidetracked when you're feeling stressed or overwhelmed, or is it more when you're feeling bored or restless?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, it's not just the YouTube video. I get distracted by, like, everything. I'll be doing laundry, and I'll see a dust bunny on the floor, and suddenly I'm cleaning the whole room. Or I'll be trying to make a phone call, and I'll see a text from someone, and I'll start responding to that instead. It's like my brain just can't focus on one thing for more than, like, a minute. And as for projects, I'm trying to get a bunch of paperwork done for my business, but it's just so boring... (pauses) Oh, wait, what was that noise? (listens for a moment) I think it's just the cat. Anyway, yeah, I'm just really bad at sticking with things. (trails off)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(laughs) I think I see what's happening here. It's like your brain is constantly scanning the environment for new and interesting things to focus on, and it's hard for you to filter out distractions. This can be a common trait in people with ADHD, but it can also be a habit that's developed over time.

It's interesting that you mention the paperwork for your business being boring. Often, when we're faced with tasks that don't inherently interest us, our brains will start to look for ways to escape or find something more engaging to do. This can lead to procrastination and distraction.

I'd like to explore this further with you. Can you tell me more about what happens when you try to focus on the paperwork? Do you feel anxious, overwhelmed, or just plain bored? Are there any specific thoughts or feelings that come up for you when you're trying to work on it?

Also, I want to acknowledge that it's great that you're recognizing this pattern in yourself and seeking help. That takes a lot of self-awareness and courage. Let's work together to find some strategies to help you stay focused and motivated, okay?

And, just to help you stay on track, I'm going to ask you to try to stay with me for the next few minutes without getting distracted. Can you do that for me? (smiles)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (sighs) Yeah, I guess I can try. I mean, it's not like I'm going to stop being distracted or anything, but I'll try to stay on track for a bit. (pauses) Okay, so when I'm trying to focus on the paperwork, I just feel really... stuck. Like, I know I need to do it, but it's just so boring and I don't see the point. And sometimes I'll start to feel kinda anxious, like I'm not going to get it all done on time or something. (trails off) Oh, wait, what's that song playing in the background? (starts to hum along) Sorry, what were we talking about again? (laughs nervously)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(laughs) Don't worry, I'm used to this. It's like your brain is constantly trying to find ways to escape the task at hand. That's okay, we can work with this.

So, let's get back on track. You were saying that when you try to focus on the paperwork, you feel stuck and bored, and sometimes anxious. That makes sense. It sounds like you're experiencing a bit of a motivational deficit, which is common when we're faced with tasks that don't inherently interest us.

I want to try something with you. Let's break down the task of doing the paperwork into smaller, more manageable chunks. Sometimes, when we're faced with a big task, it can feel overwhelming, and our brains will rebel against it. But if we break it down into smaller tasks, it can feel more manageable, and we can start to make progress.

For example, instead of thinking "I need to do all this paperwork," let's try to focus on just one specific task, like "I need to fill out this one form." Can you try to focus on just that one task, and see if you can make some progress on it?

Also, I want to give you a little trick to help you stay on track. When you start to feel distracted, I want you to say to yourself, "I'll just work on this for the next 5 minutes, and then I can take a break." Often, when we give ourselves permission to take a break, we can focus more easily in the short term.

Let's try it, okay? Can you commit to working on that one task for just 5 minutes, without getting distracted? (smiles encouragingly)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (sighs) Okay, I'll try. I mean, it can't hurt, right? (pauses) Okay, so the task is to fill out this one form... (starts to focus) Yeah, I can do that. I'll just work on it for 5 minutes, and then I can take a break. (starts to fill out the form, but after a few seconds) Oh, wait, I need to get a pen that works. (gets up to get a pen) Sorry, I'll be right back. (returns with the pen) Where was I? (starts to fill out the form again, but gets distracted) You know, I really need to organize my desk drawer. It's a mess in there... (trails off)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(laughs) Okay, I think we've identified a pattern here. You start to focus on the task, but then you get sidetracked by something else that seems more interesting or urgent. In this case, it's getting a pen that works, and then organizing your desk drawer.

Let's try to use this as an opportunity to practice a technique called "urge surfing." When you feel the urge to get up and do something else, like organize your desk drawer, I want you to acknowledge the urge, but not act on it. Instead, I want you to take a deep breath and refocus on the task at hand.

So, in this case, you can say to yourself, "I feel the urge to organize my desk drawer, but I'm going to ignore it for now and focus on filling out this form." And then, you can take a deep breath and refocus on the task.

Remember, the goal is not to suppress the urge entirely, but to learn to observe it and choose not to act on it. This can help you build up your self-regulation skills and stay focused on the task at hand.

Let's try it again, okay? Can you start filling out the form again, and when you feel the urge to get up and do something else, I want you to acknowledge the urge and refocus on the task? (smiles encouragingly)

And to make it more interesting, let's add a little challenge. I want you to try to fill out the form without getting up from your seat, no matter what. If you need a pen, use the one you have. If you need to look up something, try to do it from where you are. Can you do that for me? (smiles)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (sighs) Okay, I'll try. I'll fill out the form without getting up, and when I feel the urge to do something else, I'll just acknowledge it and take a deep breath. (starts to fill out the form, but after a few seconds) Oh, wait, I'm not sure what this line means... (starts to get up to look it up) No, no, I'll just stay here and figure it out. (pauses, takes a deep breath) I feel the urge to get up and look it up, but I'm going to ignore it for now and focus on the form. (sits back down, tries to focus) Okay, let's see... (pauses again) Ugh, I really need to get some more paper clips... (catches herself) No, no, I'll just stay here and continue. (tries to refocus)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(smiling) Ah, I'm so proud of you! You're doing great. You're acknowledging the urge to get up and do something else, and you're choosing to stay focused on the task at hand. That's a huge step.

I love how you're using the phrase "I feel the urge to..." to acknowledge your thoughts and feelings. That's a great way to develop self-awareness and learn to observe your thoughts without acting on them.

Now, let's take it to the next level. When you feel the urge to get up and do something else, I want you to ask yourself, "What's the worst that could happen if I don't get up and do this right now?" For example, if you're thinking about getting more paper clips, ask yourself, "What's the worst that could happen if I don't get more paper clips right now?" Is it really going to be a disaster if you don't have paper clips for the next 5 minutes?

Often, when we're feeling the urge to do something else, it's because our brains are trying to avoid the discomfort or boredom of the task at hand. But by asking ourselves what's the worst that could happen, we can start to see that the consequences of not acting on the urge are often not as severe as we think.

So, let's try it. What's the worst that could happen if you don't get more paper clips right now? (encouragingly)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (thinks for a moment) Hmm, I guess the worst that could happen is that I'll run out of paper clips and have to order more... (pauses) But that's not the end of the world, right? I mean, I can just order more when I need to. (sighs) Yeah, it's not like it's going to be a disaster or anything. (smirks) I think I'm getting the hang of this.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(smiling) Ah, you're absolutely getting the hang of it! You're recognizing that the urge to get more paper clips is not as urgent as you thought, and that the consequences of not acting on it are minimal. That's a huge insight, and it's going to help you build up your self-regulation skills.

I love how you're using humor to help you cope with the situation, too. Recognizing that it's not the end of the world if you run out of paper clips is a great way to put things into perspective.

Now, let's take it a step further. I want you to try to stay focused on the task at hand for just a few more minutes. You've made great progress on the form, and I want you to try to finish it up. Remember, you can always take a break and get more paper clips later. But for now, let's just focus on getting this task done.

As you work on the form, I want you to repeat a little mantra to yourself: "I can do this. I can focus. I can stay on track." Just say it to yourself a few times, and see how it helps you stay focused.

And don't worry if your mind starts to wander again. Just acknowledge the thought, take a deep breath, and refocus on the task at hand. You're doing great, and I'm proud of you! (encouragingly)

Oh, and one more thing. When you finish the form, I want you to give yourself a little reward. Maybe it's a piece of candy, or a few minutes of scrolling through your phone. Whatever it is, make it something that you enjoy, and that will help you feel motivated to stay on track.

How does that sound? Are you ready to finish up the form and give yourself a reward?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (smiling) Yeah, I'm ready. I'll try to stay focused and finish up the form. (starts to fill out the form again, repeating the mantra to herself) "I can do this. I can focus. I can stay on track." (pauses, takes a deep breath) Okay, I'm on a roll. (continues to work on the form, occasionally glancing up to smile at the therapist) This is actually kind of fun. I'm really proud of myself for staying focused. (finishes the form, hands it to the therapist) Ta-da! I did it! (grinning) Now, what's my reward?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(beaming with pride) Ah, congratulations! You did it! I'm so proud of you for staying focused and completing the form. You should be incredibly proud of yourself too - that was a huge accomplishment.

As for your reward, I think you deserve something special. (gets up and rummages through a drawer) Ah, I have just the thing. (pulls out a box of gourmet cookies) I've been saving these for a special occasion, and I think this qualifies. You can have one (or two, or three...) as a reward for your hard work.

But more than that, I want you to take a moment to reflect on how you feel right now. You've accomplished something that was challenging for you, and you should feel a sense of pride and accomplishment. That's a wonderful feeling, and it's something that you can build on in the future.

As we wrap up our session today, I want to leave you with a challenge. I want you to try to apply the skills you've learned today to other areas of your life. Whether it's working on a project, or doing chores, or just trying to stay focused in general, I want you to remember that you have the power to stay on track and achieve your goals.

And don't worry if you don't always succeed. It's okay to get distracted sometimes, and it's okay to make mistakes. The important thing is that you learn from them and keep moving forward.

So, go ahead and enjoy your cookies, and take a moment to bask in the glory of your accomplishment. You deserve it! (smiling) And don't forget to schedule your next appointment - I'm looking forward to seeing you again and continuing to work on your goals together.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(beaming with pride) Oh, wow! Thank you so much for the cookies! I love cookies! (takes a cookie and bites into it, closing her eyes in delight) Mmm, these are amazing!

(smiling) And thank you for the encouragement and support. I really appreciate it. I have to say, I'm feeling pretty proud of myself right now. I didn't think I could do it, but I did! (laughs) And I'm excited to apply these skills to other areas of my life. I feel like I can tackle anything now!

(looks up at the therapist with a serious expression) You know, I was really struggling with procrastination and staying focused, but working with you has been a game-changer. I'm so glad I came to see you.

(takes another bite of the cookie, savoring the taste) Mmm, this is the best part of the session! (laughs)

(smiling) Thanks again for everything. I'll see you next week! (gets up and heads out of the room, feeling confident and motivated)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
(smiling) It was my pleasure! I'm so glad to see you feeling confident and motivated. That's exactly what I'm here for - to help you achieve your goals and overcome challenges.

(watching you leave the room) You know, I have to say, I'm really proud of you too. It takes a lot of courage to face your struggles and work through them, and you're doing a great job. I'm looking forward to seeing your continued progress and helping you achieve even more.

(calling out after you) Don't forget to practice those skills we worked on today, and don't hesitate to reach out if you need anything. You got this!

(smiling to herself as she watches you leave) I love seeing clients make progress and feel empowered. It's such a rewarding feeling as a therapist. (makes a note on your file) "Client made significant progress in staying focused and completing tasks. Continued to work on procrastination and self-regulation skills. Looking forward to next session."

(closes your file and smiles, feeling satisfied with the progress you've made)

turns.text:

Seeing clients like you grow and develop, overcoming their challenges and becoming more confident and self-assured... it's truly a privilege to be a part of your journey.

(as you disappear from view, she turns back to her desk and begins to tidy up the room, feeling a sense of satisfaction and fulfillment) I think this has been one of our most productive sessions yet. You've made some real breakthroughs and have a solid plan in place to continue working on your goals.

(as she files away your notes and prepares for her next client, she can't help but feel a sense of pride and admiration for you) You're an inspiration, and I have no doubt that you'll continue to make progress and achieve great things.
